entries.e19ac47bb93c970b14ba8e3795e78d85f59b1d11: <div sID="gen10595" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="Ps.16" sID="Ps.16"/> <div eID="gen10595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10596" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10597" type="x-p"/> This psalm has something of David in it, but much more of Christ. It begins with such expressions of devotion as may be applied to Christ; but concludes with such confidence of a resurrection (and so timely a one as to prevent corruption) as must be applied to Christ, to him only, and cannot be understood of David, as both St. Peter and St. Paul have observed, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.24">Acts ii. 24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.36">xiii. 36</reference>. For David died, and was buried, and saw corruption. I. David speaks of himself as a member of Christ, and so he speaks the language of all good Christians, professing his confidence in God ( <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">ver. 1</reference>), his consent to him ( <reference osisRef="Ps.16.2">ver. 2</reference>), his affection to the people of God ( <reference osisRef="Ps.16.3">ver. 3</reference>), his adherence to the true worship of God ( <reference osisRef="Ps.16.4">ver. 4</reference>), and his entire complacency and satisfaction in God and the interest he had in him, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.5-Ps.16.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. II. He speaks of himself as a type of Christ, and so he speaks the language of Christ himself, to whom all the rest of the psalm is expressly and at large applied (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.25-Acts.2.28">Acts ii. 25</reference>, &c.). David speaks concerning him (not concerning himself), "I foresaw the Lord always before my face," &c. And this he spoke, being a prophet, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.30-Acts.2.31">ver. 30, 31</reference>. He spoke, 1. Of the special presence of God with the Redeemer in his services and sufferings, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.8">ver. 8</reference>. 2. Of the prospect which the Redeemer had of his own resurrection and the glory that should follow, which carried him cheerfully through his undertaking, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.9-Ps.16.11">ver. 9-11</reference>.
entries.a8facf92994f6ba38065bc9fba6c5d3bbbb41adb: <div eID="gen10597" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10596" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Believing Confidence; Consecration to God.</title> <div sID="gen10598" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Preserve me, O God: for in thee do I put my trust. <hi type="super">2</hi> <hi type="italic">O my soul,</hi> thou hast said unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my Lord: my goodness <hi type="italic">extendeth</hi> not to thee; <hi type="super">3</hi> <hi type="italic">But</hi> to the saints that <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the earth, and <hi type="italic">to</hi> the excellent, in whom <hi type="italic">is</hi> all my delight. <hi type="super">4</hi> Their sorrows shall be multiplied <hi type="italic">that</hi> hasten <hi type="italic">after</hi> another <hi type="italic">god:</hi> their drink offerings of blood will I not offer, nor take up their names into my lips. <hi type="super">5</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> the portion of mine inheritance and of my cup: thou maintainest my lot. <hi type="super">6</hi> The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant <hi type="italic">places;</hi> yea, I have a goodly heritage. <hi type="super">7</hi> I will bless the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , who hath given me counsel: my reins also instruct me in the night seasons. <div eID="gen10598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10599" type="x-p"/> This psalm is entitled <hi type="italic">Michtam,</hi> which some translate <hi type="italic">a golden</hi> psalm, a very precious one, more to be valued by us than gold, yea, than much fine gold, because it speaks so plainly of Christ and his resurrection, who is the true treasure hidden in the field of the Old Testament. <div eID="gen10599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10600" type="x-p"/> I. David here flies to God's protection with a cheerful believing confidence in it (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">v. 1</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Preserve me, O God!</hi> from the deaths, and especially from the sins, to which I am continually exposed; <hi type="italic">for in thee,</hi> and in thee only, <hi type="italic">do I put my trust.</hi>" Those that by faith commit themselves to the divine care, and submit themselves to the divine guidance, have reason to hope for the benefit of both. This is applicable to Christ, who prayed, <hi type="italic">Father, save me from this hour,</hi> and trusted in God that he would deliver him. <div eID="gen10600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10601" type="x-p"/> II. He recognizes his solemn dedication of himself to God as his God (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.2">v. 2</reference>): "<hi type="italic">O my soul! thou hast said unto the Lord, Thou art my Lord,</hi> and therefore thou mayest venture to trust him." Note, 1. It is the duty and interest of every one of us to acknowledge the Lord for our Lord, to subject ourselves to him, and then to stay ourselves upon him. <hi type="italic">Adonai</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">My stayer,</hi> the strength of my heart. 2. This must be done with our souls: "O my soul! thou hast said it." Covenanting with God must be heart-work; all that is within us must be employed therein and engaged thereby. 3. Those who have avouched the Lord for their Lord should be often putting themselves in mind of what they have done. "Hast thou said unto the Lord, <hi type="italic">Thou art my Lord?</hi> Say it again then, stand to it, abide by it, and never unsay it. Hast thou said it? Take the comfort of it, and live up to it. He is thy Lord, and worship thou him, and let thy eye be ever towards him." <div eID="gen10601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10602" type="x-p"/> III. He devotes himself to the honour of God in the service of the saints (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.2-Ps.16.3">v. 2, 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">My goodness extends not to thee, but to the saints.</hi> Observe, 1. Those that have taken the lord for their Lord must, like him, be good and do good; we do not expect happiness without goodness. 2. Whatever good there is in us, or is done by us, we must humbly acknowledge that it extends not to God; so that we cannot pretend to merit any thing by it. God has no need of our services; he is not benefited by them, nor can they add any thing to his infinite perfection and blessedness. The wisest, and best, and most useful, men in the world cannot be profitable to God, <reference osisRef="Job.22.2">Job xxii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.35.7">xxxv. 7</reference>. God is infinitely above us, and happy without us, and whatever good we do it is all from him; so that we are indebted to him, not he to us: David owns it (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.14">1 Chron. xxix. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">Of thy own have we given thee.</hi> 3. If God be ours, we must, for his sake, extend our goodness to those that are his, to the saints in the earth; for what is done to them he is pleased to take as done to himself, having constituted them his receivers. Note, (1.) There are saints in the earth; and saints on earth we must all be, or we shall never be saints in heaven. Those that are renewed by the grace of God, and devoted to the glory of God, are saints on earth. (2.) The saints in the earth are excellent ones, great, mighty, magnificent ones, and yet some of them so poor in the world that they need to have David's goodness extended to them. God makes them excellent by the grace he gives them. <hi type="italic">The righteous is more excellent than his neighbour,</hi> and then he accounts them excellent. They are precious in his sight and honourable; they are his jewels, his peculiar treasure. Their God is their glory, and a diadem of beauty to them. (3.) All that have taken the Lord for their God delight in his saints as excellent ones, because they bear his image, and because he loves them. David, though a king, was a <hi type="italic">companion of all that feared God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.63">Ps. cxix. 63</reference>), even the meanest, which was a sign that his delight was in them. (4.) It is not enough for us to delight in the saints, but, as there is occasion, our goodness must extend to them; we must be ready to show them the kindness they need, distribute to their necessities, and abound in the labour of love to them. This is applicable to Christ. The salvation he wrought out for us was no gain to God, for our ruin would have been no loss to him; but the goodness and benefit of it extend to us men, in whom he delighteth, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.31">Prov. viii. 31</reference>. <hi type="italic">For their sakes,</hi> says he, <hi type="italic">I sanctify myself,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.19">John xvii. 19</reference>. Christ delights even in the saints on earth, notwithstanding their weaknesses and manifold infirmities, which is a good reason why we should. <div eID="gen10602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10603" type="x-p"/> IV. He disclaims the worship of all false gods and all communion with their worshippers, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.4">v. 4</reference>. Here, 1. He reads the doom of idolaters, who hasten after another God, being mad upon their idols, and pursuing them as eagerly as if they were afraid they would escape from them: <hi type="italic">Their sorrows shall be multiplied,</hi> both by the judgments they bring upon themselves from the true God whom they forsake and by the disappointment they will meet with in the false gods they embrace. Those that multiply gods multiply griefs to themselves; for, whoever thinks one God too little, will find two too many, and yet hundreds not enough. 2. He declares his resolution to have no fellowship with them nor with their unfruitful works of darkness: "<hi type="italic">Their drink-offerings of blood will I not offer,</hi> not only because the gods they are offered to are a lie, but because the offerings themselves are barbarous." At God's altar, because the blood made atonement, the drinking of it was most strictly prohibited, and the drink-offerings were of wine; but the devil prescribed to his worshippers to drink of the blood of the sacrifices, to teach them cruelty. "I will have nothing to do" (says David) "with those bloody deities, nor so much as take their names into my lips with any delight in them or respect to them." Thus must we hate idols and idolatry with a perfect hatred. Some make this also applicable to Christ and his undertaking, showing the nature of the sacrifice he offered (it was not the blood of bulls and goats, which was offered according to the law; that was never named, nor did he ever make any mention of it, but his own blood), showing also the multiplied sorrows of the unbelieving Jews, who hastened after another king, Cæsar, and are still hastening after another Messiah, whom they in vain look for. <div eID="gen10603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10604" type="x-p"/> V. He repeats the solemn choice he had made of God for his portion and happiness (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">v. 5</reference>), takes to himself the comfort of the choice (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.6">v. 6</reference>), and gives God the glory of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.7">v. 7</reference>. This is very much the language of a devout and pious soul in its gracious exercises. <div eID="gen10604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10605" type="x-p"/> 1. Choosing the Lord for its portion and happiness. "Most men take the world for their chief good, and place their felicity in the enjoyments of it; but this I say, <hi type="italic">The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup,</hi> the portion I make choice of, and will gladly take up with, how poor soever my condition is in this world. Let me have the love and favour of God, and be accepted of him; let me have the comfort of communion with God, and satisfaction in the communications of his graces and comforts; let me have an interest in his promises, and a title by promise to everlasting life and happiness in the future state; and I have enough, I need no more, I desire no more, to complete my felicity." Would we do well and wisely for ourselves, we must take God, in Christ, to be, (1.) The portion of our inheritance in the other world. Heaven is an inheritance. God himself is the inheritance of the saints there, whose everlasting bliss is to enjoy him. We must take that for our inheritance, our home, our rest, our lasting, everlasting, good, and look upon this world to be no more ours than the country through which our road lies when we are on a journey. (2.) The portion of our cup in this world, with which we are nourished, and refreshed, and kept from fainting. Those have not God for theirs who do not reckon his comforts the most reviving cordials, acquaint themselves with them, and make use of them as sufficient to counterbalance all the grievances of this present time and to sweeten the most bitter cup of affliction. <div eID="gen10605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10606" type="x-p"/> 2. Confiding in him for the securing of this portion: "<hi type="italic">Thou maintainest my lot.</hi> Thou that hast by promise made over thy self to me, to be mine, wilt graciously make good what thou hast promised, and never leave me to myself to forfeit this happiness, nor leave it in the power of my enemies to rob me of it. Nothing shall pluck me out of thy hands, nor separate me from thy love, and the sure mercies of David." The saints and their bliss are kept by the power of God. <div eID="gen10606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10607" type="x-p"/> 3. Rejoicing in this portion, and taking a complacency in it (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places.</hi> Those have reason to say so that have God for their portion; they have a worthy portion, a goodly heritage. What can they have better? What can they desire more? <hi type="italic">Return unto thy rest, O my soul!</hi> and look no further. Note, Gracious persons, though they still covet more of God, never covet more than God; but, being satisfied of his loving-kindness, they are abundantly satisfied with it, and envy not any their carnal mirth and sensual pleasures and delights, but account themselves truly happy in what they have, and doubt not but to be completely happy in what they hope for. Those whose lot is cast, as David's was, in a land of light, in a valley of vision, where God is known and worshipped, have, upon that account, reason to say, <hi type="italic">The lines have fallen to me in pleasant places;</hi> much more those who have not only the means, but the end, not only Immanuel's land, but Immanuel's love. <div eID="gen10607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10608" type="x-p"/> 4. Giving thanks to God for it, and for grace to make this wise and happy choice (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.7">v. 7</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will bless the Lord who has given me counsel,</hi> this counsel, to take him for my portion and happiness." So ignorant and foolish are we that, if we be left to ourselves, our hearts will follow our eyes, and we shall choose our own delusions, and forsake our own mercies for lying vanities; and therefore, if we have indeed taken God for our portion and preferred spiritual and eternal blessings before those that are sensible and temporal, we must thankfully acknowledge the power and goodness of divine grace directing and enabling us to make that choice. If we have the pleasure of it, let God have the praise of it. <div eID="gen10608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10609" type="x-p"/> 5. Making a good use of it. God having given him counsel by his word and Spirit, his own <hi type="italic">reins</hi> also (his own thoughts) instructed him in the night-season; when he was silent and solitary, and retired from the world, then his own conscience (which is called the <hi type="italic">reins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.17.10">Jer. xvii. 10</reference>) not only reflected with comfort upon the choice he had made, but instructed or admonished him concerning the duties arising out of this choice, catechized him, and engaged and quickened him to live as one that had God for his portion, by faith to live upon him and to live to him. Those who have God for their portion, and who will be faithful to him, must give their own consciences leave to deal thus faithfully and plainly with them. <div eID="gen10609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10610" type="x-p"/> All this may be applied to Christ, who made the Lord his portion and was pleased with that portion, made his Father's glory his highest end and made it his meat and drink to seek that and to do his will, and delighted to prosecute his undertaking, pursuant to his Father's counsel, depending upon him to maintain his lot and to carry him through his undertaking. We may also apply it to ourselves in singing it, renewing our choice of God as ours, with a holy complacency and satisfaction.
entries.cb8b11ef650a69ab73888e9aea5690bb7568c4ae: <div eID="gen10610" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prophecy Relating to the Messiah; Sufferings and Consequent Glory of Christ.</title> <div sID="gen10611" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> I have set the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> always before me: because <hi type="italic">he is</hi> at my right hand, I shall not be moved. <hi type="super">9</hi> Therefore my heart is glad, and my glory rejoiceth: my flesh also shall rest in hope. 10 For thou wilt not leave my soul in hell; neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption. <hi type="super">11</hi> Thou wilt show me the path of life: in thy presence <hi type="italic">is</hi> fulness of joy; at thy right hand <hi type="italic">there are</hi> pleasures for evermore. <div eID="gen10611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10612" type="x-p"/> All these verses are quoted by St. Peter in his first sermon, after the pouring out of the Spirit on the day of pentecost (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.25-Acts.2.28">Acts ii. 25-28</reference>); and he tells us expressly that David in them speaks concerning Christ and particularly of his resurrection. Something we may allow here of the workings of David's own pious and devout affections towards God, depending upon his grace to perfect every thing that concerned him, and looking for the blessed hope, and happy state on the other side death, in the enjoyment of God; but in these holy elevations towards God and heaven he was carried by the spirit of prophecy quite beyond the consideration of himself and his own case, to foretel the glory of the Messiah, in such expressions as were peculiar to that, and could not be understood of himself. The New Testament furnishes us with a key to let us into the mystery of these lines. <div eID="gen10612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10613" type="x-p"/> I. These verses must certainly be applied to Christ; of him speaks the prophet this, as did many of the Old-Testament prophets, who <hi type="italic">testified beforehand the sufferings of Christ and the glory that should follow</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 11</reference>), and that is the subject of this prophecy here. It is foretold (as he himself showed concerning this, no doubt, among other prophecies in this psalm, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.44">Luke xxiv. 44</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.46">46</reference>) that <hi type="italic">Christ should suffer, and rise from the dead,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.3-1Cor.15.4">1 Cor. xv. 3, 4</reference>. <div eID="gen10613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10614" type="x-p"/> 1. That he should suffer and die. This is implied here when he says (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">I shall not be moved;</hi> he supposed that he should be struck at, and have a dreadful shock given him, as he had in his agony, when his soul was exceedingly sorrowful, and he prayed that the cup might pass from him. When he says, "<hi type="italic">My flesh shall rest,</hi>" it is implied that he must put off the body, and therefore must go through the pains of death. It is likewise plainly intimated that his soul must go into a state of separation from the body, and that his body, so deserted, would be in imminent danger of seeing corruption—that he should not only die, but be buried, and abide for some time under the power of death. <div eID="gen10614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10615" type="x-p"/> 2. That he should be wonderfully borne up by the divine power in suffering and dying. (1.) That he should not be moved, should not be driven off from his undertaking nor sink under the weight of it, that he should not fail nor be discouraged (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.4">Isa. xlii. 4</reference>), but should proceed and persevere in it, till he could say, <hi type="italic">It is finished.</hi> Though the service was hard and the encounter hot, and he trod the winepress alone, yet he was not moved, did not give up the cause, but set his face as a flint, <reference osisRef="Isa.50.7-Isa.50.9">Isa. l. 7-9</reference>. <hi type="italic">Here am I, let these go their way.</hi> Nay, (2.) That his heart should rejoice and his glory be glad, that he should go on with his undertaking, not only resolutely, but cheerfully, and with unspeakable pleasure and satisfaction, witness that saying (<reference osisRef="John.17.11">John xvii. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">Now I am no more in the world, but I come to thee,</hi> and that (<reference osisRef="John.18.11">John xviii. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">The cup that my Father has given me, shall I not drink it?</hi> and many the like. By his glory is meant his <hi type="italic">tongue,</hi> as appears, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.26">Acts ii. 26</reference>. For our tongue is our glory, and never more so than when it is employed in glorifying God. Now there were three things which bore him up and carried him on thus cheerfully:—[1.] The respect he had to his Father's will and glory in what he did: <hi type="italic">I have set the Lord always before me.</hi> He still had an eye to his Father's commandment (<reference osisRef="John.10.18">John x. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.31">xiv. 31</reference>), the will of him that sent him. He aimed at his Father's honour and the restoring of the interests of his kingdom among men, and this kept him from being moved by the difficulties he met with; for he always did those things that pleased his Father. [2.] The assurance he had of his Father's presence with him in his sufferings: <hi type="italic">He is at my right hand,</hi> a present help to me, nigh at hand in the time of need. <hi type="italic">He is near that justifieth me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.8">Isa. l. 8</reference>); he is at my right hand, to direct and strengthen it, and hold it up, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.21">Ps. lxxxix. 21</reference>. When he was in his agony an angel was sent from heaven to strengthen him, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.43">Luke xxii. 43</reference>. To this the victories and triumphs of the cross were all owing; it was the Lord at his right hand that <hi type="italic">struck through kings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.5">Ps. cx. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1-Isa.42.2">Isa. xlii. 1, 2</reference>. [3.] The prospect he had of a glorious issue of his sufferings. It was <hi type="italic">for the joy set before him</hi> that <hi type="italic">he endured the cross,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">Heb. xii. 2</reference>. He rested in hope, and that made his rest glorious, <reference osisRef="Isa.11.10">Isa. xi. 10</reference>. He knew he should be justified in the Spirit by his resurrection, and straightway glorified. See <reference osisRef="John.13.31-John.13.32">John xiii. 31, 32</reference>. <div eID="gen10615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10616" type="x-p"/> 3. That he should be brought through his sufferings, and brought from under the power of death by a glorious resurrection. (1.) That his soul should not be left in hell, that is, his human spirit should not be long left, as other men's spirits are, in a state of separation from the body, but should, in a little time, return and be re-united to it, never to part again. (2.) That being God's holy One in a peculiar manner, sanctified to the work of redemption and perfectly free from sin, he should not see corruption nor feel it. This implies that he should not only be raised from the grave, but raised so soon that his dead body should not so much as being to corrupt, which, in the course of nature, it would have done if it had not been raised the third day. We, who have so much corruption in our souls, must expect that our bodies also will corrupt (<reference osisRef="Job.24.19">Job xxiv. 19</reference>); but that holy One of God who knew no sin saw no corruption. Under the law it was strictly ordered that those parts of the sacrifices which were not burnt upon the altar should by no means be kept till the third day, lest they should putrefy (<reference osisRef="Lev.7.15">Lev. vii. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.18">18</reference>), which perhaps pointed at Christ's rising the third day, that he might not see corruption—neither was a bone of him broken. <div eID="gen10616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10617" type="x-p"/> 4. That he should be abundantly recompensed for his sufferings, with the joy set before him, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.11">v. 11</reference>. He was well assured, (1.) That he should not miss of his glory: "<hi type="italic">Thou wilt show me the path of life,</hi> and lead me to that life through this darksome valley." In confidence of this, when he gave up the ghost, he said, <hi type="italic">Father, into thy hands I commit my spirit;</hi> and, a little before, <hi type="italic">Father, glorify me with thy own self.</hi> (2.) That he should be received into the presence of God, to sit at his right hand. His being admitted into God's presence would be the acceptance of his service and his being set at his right hand the recompence of it. (3.) Thus, as a reward for the sorrows he underwent for our redemption, he should have a <hi type="italic">fulness of joy, and pleasures for evermore;</hi> not only the glory he had with God, as God, before all worlds, but the joy and pleasure of a Mediator, in seeing his seed, and the success and prosperity of his undertaking, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10-Isa.53.11">Isa. liii. 10, 11</reference>. <div eID="gen10617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10618" type="x-p"/> II. Christ being the Head of the body, the church, these verses may, for the most part, be applied to all good Christians, who are guided and animated by the Spirit of Christ; and, in singing them, when we have first given glory to Christ, in whom, to our everlasting comfort, they have had their accomplishment, we may then encourage and edify ourselves and one another with them, and may hence learn, 1. That it is our wisdom and duty to set the Lord always before us, and to see him continually at our right hand, wherever we are, to eye him as our chief good and highest end, our owner, ruler, and judge, our gracious benefactor, our sure guide and strict observer; and, while we do thus, we shall not be moved either from our duty or from our comfort. Blessed Paul set the Lord before him, when, though bonds and afflictions did await him, he could bravely say, <hi type="italic">None of these things move me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.20.24">Acts xx. 24</reference>. 2. That, if our eyes be ever towards God, our hearts and tongues may ever rejoice in him; it is our own fault if they do not. If the heart rejoice in God, out of the abundance of that let the mouth speak, to his glory, and the edification of others. 3. That dying Christians, as well as a dying Christ, may cheerfully put off the body, in a believing expectation of a joyful resurrection: <hi type="italic">My flesh also shall rest in hope.</hi> Our bodies have little rest in this world, but in the grave they shall rest as in their beds, <reference osisRef="Isa.57.2">Isa. lvii. 2</reference>. We have little to hope for from this life, but we shall rest in hope of a better life; we may put off the body in that hope. Death <hi type="italic">destroys the hope of man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.14.19">Job xiv. 19</reference>), but not the hope of a good Christian, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.32">Prov. xiv. 32</reference>. He has hope in his death, living hopes in dying moments, hopes that the body shall not be left for ever in the grave, but, though it see corruption for a time, it shall, at the end of the time, be raised to immortality; Christ's resurrection is an earnest of ours if we be his. 4. That those who live piously with God in their eye may die comfortably with heaven in their eye. In this world sorrow is our lot, but in heaven there is joy. All our joys here are empty and defective, but in heaven there is a fulness of joy. Our pleasures here are transient and momentary, and such is the nature of them that it is not fit they should last long; but those at God's right hand are pleasures for evermore; for they are the pleasures of immortal souls in the immediate vision and fruition of an eternal God.  <chapter eID="Ps.16"/> <div eID="gen10618" type="x-p"/>

entries.88f2d547f744b2655ec84834ac394c0c9f9c0f05: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5588"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 16</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.16.1-Ps.16.11">Psa 16:1-11</reference>. Michtam, or, by the change of one letter, Michtab--a "writing," such as a poem or song (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.38.9">Is 38:9</reference>). Such a change of the letter m for b was not unusual. The position of this word in connection with the author's name, being that usually occupied by some term, such as Psalm or song, denoting the style or matter of the composition, favors this view of its meaning, though we know not why this and Psalms 56-60 should be specially, called "a writing." "A</title> <div sID="gen8490" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">golden (Psalm)," or "a memorial" are explanations proposed by some--</hi>neither of which, however applicable here, appears adapted to the other Psalms where the term occurs. According to Peter (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.25">Ac 2:25</reference>) and Paul (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.35">Ac 13:35</reference>), this Psalm relates to Christ and expresses the feelings of His human nature, in view of His sufferings and victory over death and the grave, including His subsequent exaltation at the right hand of God. Such was the exposition of the best earlier Christian interpreters. Some moderns have held that the Psalm relates exclusively to David; but this view is expressly contradicted by the apostles; others hold that the language of the Psalm is applicable to David as a type of Christ, capable of the higher sense assigned it in the New Testament. But then the language of <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Psa 16:10</reference> cannot be used of David in any sense, for "he saw corruption." Others again propose to refer the first part to David, and the last to Christ; but it is evident that no change in the subject of the Psalm is indicated. Indeed, the person who appeals to God for help is evidently the same who rejoices in having found it. In referring the whole Psalm to Christ, it is, however, by no means denied that much of its language is expressive of the feelings of His people, so far as in their humble measure they have the feelings of trust in God expressed by Him, their head and representative. Such use of His language, as recorded in His last prayer (<reference osisRef="John.17.1-John.17.26">Joh 17:1-26</reference>), and even that which He used in Gethsemane, under similar modifications, is equally proper. The propriety of this reference of the Psalm to Christ will appear in the scope and interpretation. In view of the sufferings before Him, the Saviour, with that instinctive dread of death manifested in Gethsemane, calls on God to "preserve" Him; He avows His delight in holiness and abhorrence of the wicked and their wickedness; and for "the joy that was set before Him, despising the shame" [He 12:2], encourages Himself; contemplating the glories of the heritage appointed Him. Thus even death and the grave lose their terrors in the assurance of the victory to be attained and "the glory that should follow" [1Pe 1:11].<div eID="gen8490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8491" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5588"/><hi type="bold">1. Preserve me, &c.--</hi>keep or watch over my interests.<div eID="gen8491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8492" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in thee ... I ... trust--</hi>as one seeking shelter from pressing danger. <div eID="gen8492" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8c3d6540e3a7c8c3846215a4ed37d3871db3cd7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5589"/><div sID="gen8493" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5589"/><hi type="bold">2. my soul--</hi>must be supplied; expressed in similar cases (<reference osisRef="Ps.42.5">Psa 42:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.11">11</reference>).<div eID="gen8493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my goodness ... thee--</hi>This obscure passage is variously expounded. Either one of two expositions falls in with the context. "My goodness" or merit is not on account of Thee--that is, is not for Thy benefit. Then follows the contrast of <reference osisRef="Ps.16.3">Psa 16:3</reference> (but is), in respect, or for the saints, &c.--that is, it enures to them. Or, my goodness--or happiness is not besides Thee--that is, without Thee I have no other source of happiness. Then, "to the saints," &c., means that the same privilege of deriving happiness from God only is theirs. The first is the most consonant with the Messianic character of the Psalm, though the latter is not inconsistent with it. <div eID="gen8494" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1fb79611c20706091a212e612ad877b41142a4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5590"/><div sID="gen8495" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5590"/><hi type="bold">3. saints--</hi>or, persons consecrated to God, set apart from others to His service.<div eID="gen8495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the earth--</hi>that is, land of Palestine, the residence of God's chosen people--figuratively for the Church.<div eID="gen8496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">excellent--</hi>or, "nobles," distinguished for moral excellence. <div eID="gen8497" type="x-p"/>
entries.189f484260402821f7d60de519e1e181f349ac4b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5591"/><div sID="gen8498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5591"/>4. He expresses his abhorrence of those who seek other sources of happiness or objects of worship, and, by characterizing their rites by drink offerings of blood, clearly denotes idolaters. The word for "sorrows" is by some rendered "idols"; but, though a similar word to that for idols, it is not the same. In selecting such a term, there may be an allusion, by the author, to the sorrows produced by idolatrous practices. <div eID="gen8498" type="x-p"/>
entries.b54b2974d1babe4f1c2fd7f10f1c0bafc1accdaa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5592"/><div sID="gen8499" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5592"/>5-7. God is the chief good, and supplies all need (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.9">De 10:9</reference>).<div eID="gen8499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">portion of mine inheritance and of my cup--</hi>may contain an allusion to the daily supply of food, and also to the inheritance of Levi (<reference osisRef="Deut.18.1">De 18:1</reference>, 2).<div eID="gen8500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8501" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">maintainest--</hi>or, drawest out my lot--enlargest it. <reference osisRef="Ps.16.7">Psa 16:7</reference> carries out this idea more fully. <div eID="gen8501" type="x-p"/>
entries.9efb7cd1af7a6dddc740f556f11f904704cad6bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5594"/><div sID="gen8505" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5594"/>8. With God's presence and aid he is sure of safety (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.6">Psa 10:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.15.5">15:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.27">Joh 12:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.12.28">28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">He 5:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.5.8">8</reference>). <div eID="gen8505" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e743c438e6cbb7449288cefba9ae7fecd40a990: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5595"/><div sID="gen8506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5595"/><hi type="bold">9. glory--</hi>as heart (<reference osisRef="Ps.7.5">Psa 7:5</reference>), for self. In <reference osisRef="Acts.2.26">Ac 2:26</reference>, after the Septuagint, "my tongue" as "the glory of the frame"--the instrument for praising God.<div eID="gen8506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flesh--</hi>If taken as opposed to soul (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Psa 16:10</reference>), it may mean the body; otherwise, the whole person (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1">Psa 63:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.2">84:2</reference>).<div eID="gen8507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rest in hope--</hi>(compare Margin). <div eID="gen8508" type="x-p"/>
entries.c5bf779f15555dc24992de6331cc0acfcbbb4d70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5596"/><div sID="gen8509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5596"/><hi type="bold">10. soul--</hi>or, "self." This use of "soul" for the person is frequent (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.5">Ge 12:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.46.26">46:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.3.2">Psa 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.7.2">7:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.11.1">11:1</reference>), even when the body may be the part chiefly affected, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.35.13">Psa 35:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.105.18">105:18</reference>. Some cases are cited, as <reference osisRef="Lev.22.4">Le 22:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.6.6">Nu 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.9.6">9:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.9.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.19.13">19:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hag.2.13">Hag 2:13</reference>, &c., which seem to justify assigning the meaning of body, or dead body; but it will be found that the latter sense is given by some adjunct expressed or implied. In those cases person is the proper sense.<div eID="gen8509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8510" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wilt not leave ... hell--</hi>abandon to the power of (<reference osisRef="Job.39.14">Job 39:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.10">Psa 49:10</reference>). Hell as (<reference osisRef="Gen.42.38">Ge 42:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.5">Psa 6:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.2">Jon 2:2</reference>) the state or region of death, and so frequently--or the grave itself (<reference osisRef="Job.14.13">Job 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.17.13">17:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.10">Ec 9:10</reference>, &c.). So the Greek Hades (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.2.27">Ac 2:27</reference>, 31). The context alone can settle whether the state mentioned is one of suffering and place of the damned (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.9.17">Psa 9:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.5.5">Pr 5:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.7.27">7:27</reference>).<div eID="gen8510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8511" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wilt ... suffer--</hi>literally, "give" or "appoint."<div eID="gen8511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8512" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Holy One--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>), one who is the object of God's favor, and so a recipient of divine grace which he exhibits--pious.<div eID="gen8512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8513" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to see--</hi>or, "experience"--undergo (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.26">Lu 2:26</reference>).<div eID="gen8513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8514" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">corruption--</hi>Some render the word, the pit, which is possible, but for the obvious sense which the apostle's exposition (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.27">Ac 2:27</reference>; 13:36, 37) gives. The sense of the whole passage is clearly this: by the use of flesh and soul, the disembodied state produced by death is indicated; but, on the other hand, no more than the state of death is intended; for the last clause of <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Psa 16:10</reference> is strictly parallel with the first, and Holy One corresponds to soul, and corruption to hell. As Holy One, or David (<reference osisRef="Acts.13.36">Ac 13:36</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.37">37</reference>), which denotes the person, including soul and body, is used for body, of which only corruption can be predicated (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.2.31">Ac 2:31</reference>); so, on the contrary, soul, which literally means the immaterial part, is used for the person. The language may be thus paraphrased, "In death I shall hope for resurrection; for I shall not be left under its dominion and within its bounds, or be subject to the corruption which ordinarily ensues." <div eID="gen8514" type="x-p"/>
entries.e205d9770d83a2c759fed311c935abf77c766361: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5597"/><div sID="gen8515" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5597"/>11. Raised from the dead, he shall die no more; death hath no more dominion over him.<div eID="gen8515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8516" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thou wilt show me--</hi>guide me to attain.<div eID="gen8516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8517" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the path of life--</hi>or, "lives"--the plural denoting variety and abundance--immortal blessedness of every sort--as "life" often denotes.<div eID="gen8517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8518" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in thy presence--</hi>or, "before Thy faces." The frequent use of this plural form for "faces" may contain an allusion to the Trinity (<reference osisRef="Num.6.25">Nu 6:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.6.26">26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">Psa 17:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.16">31:16</reference>).<div eID="gen8518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">at thy right hand--</hi>to which Christ was exalted (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Psa 110:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.33">Ac 2:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.3.1">Col 3:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.3">He 1:3</reference>). In the glories of this state, He shall see of the travail (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Is 53:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.2.9">Php 2:9</reference>) of His soul, and be satisfied. <chapter eID="Ps.16"/>

entries.af675d213c98b5aca460bde28b567ef30007013f: <div eID="gen18842" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen18843" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18844" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18844" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18843" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18845" type="x-p"/> The contents of this Psalm are usually given in the following manner: David, sojourning among idolaters, and being obliged to leave his own country through Saul's persecution, cries to God for help; expresses his abhorrence of idolatry, and his desire to be again united to God's people, <reference osisRef="Psa.16.1-Psa.16.4">Psa 16:1-4</reference>; and dedares his strong confidence in God, who had dealt bountifully with him, <reference osisRef="Psa.16.5-Psa.16.7">Psa 16:5-7</reference>. Then follows a remarkable prophecy of the resurrection of Christ, <reference osisRef="Psa.16.8-Psa.16.11">Psa 16:8-11</reference>. <div eID="gen18845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18846" type="x-p"/> The title of this Psalm in the Hebrew is מכתם לדוד michtam ledavid, which the Chaldee translates, "A straight sculpture of David." The Septuagint, Στηλογραφια τῳ Δαυιδ, "The inscription on a pillar to David;" as if the Psalm had been inscribed on a pillar, to keep it in remembrance. As כתם catham signifies to engrave or stamp, this has given rise to the above inscription. מכתם michtam also means pure or stamped gold; and hence it has been supposed that this title was given to it on account of its excellence: a golden Psalm, or a Psalm worthy to be written on letters of gold; as some of the verses of Pythagoras were called the golden verses, because of their excellence. Gold being the most excellent and precious of all metals, it has been used to express metaphorically excellence and perfection of every kind. Thus a golden tongue or mouth, the most excellent eloquence; so Chrysostom means, this eminent man having had his name from his eloquence; - a golden book, one of the choicest and most valuable of its kind, etc. But I have already sufficiently expressed my doubts concerning the meanings given to these titles. See the note on the title of <reference osisRef="Psa.60.1-Psa.60.12">Psa 60:1-12</reference> (note). <div eID="gen18846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18847" type="x-p"/> That David was the author there can be no doubt. It is most pointedly attributed to him by St. Peter, <reference osisRef="Act.2.25-Act.2.31">Act 2:25-31</reference>. That its principal parts might have some relation to his circumstances is also probable; but that Jesus Christ is its main scope, not only appears from quotations made by the apostle as above, but from the circumstance that some parts of it never did and never could apply to David. From the most serious and attentive consideration of the whole Psalm, I am convinced that every verse of it belongs to Jesus Christ, and none other: and this, on reference, I find to be the view taken of it by my ancient Psalter. But as he is referred to here as the Redeemer of the world, consequently, as God manifested in the flesh, there are several portions of the Psalm, as well as in the New Testament, where the Divine and human natures are spoken of separrately: and if this distinction be properly regarded, we shall find, not only no inconsistency, but a beautiful harmony through the whole. <div eID="gen18847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18848" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen18848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18849" type="x-p"/> Preserve me, O God: for in thee do I put my trust - On the mode of interpretation which I have hinted at above, I consider this a prayer of the man Christ Jesus on his entering on his great atoning work, particularly his passion in the garden of Gethsemane. In that passion, Jesus Christ most evidently speaks as man; and with the strictest propriety, as it was the manhood, not the Godhead, that was engaged in the suffering. שמרני shomreni, keep me - preserve, sustain, this feeble humanity, now about to bear the load of that punishment due to the whole of the human race. For in thee, חסיתי chasithi, have I hoped. No human fortitude, or animal courage, can avail in my circumstances. These are no common sufferings; they are not of a natural kind; they are not proportioned to the strength of a human body, or the energy of a human spirit; and my immaculate humanity, which is subjected to these sufferings, must be dissolved by them, if not upheld by thee, the strong God. It is worthy of remark, that our Lord here uses the term, אל El, which signifies the strong God, an expression remarkably suited to the frailty of that human nature, which was now entering upon its vicarious sufferings. It will be seen with what admirable propriety the Messiah varies the appellations of the Divine Being in this address; a circumstance which no translation without paraphrase can express.
entries.922d40387592a9a35d3caf064a3a80cdde9691b0: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen18849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18850" type="x-p"/> Thou hast said unto the Lord, Thou art my Lord - Thou hast said ליהוה layhovah to Jehovah, the supreme, self-existing, and eternal Being; Thou art my Lord, אדני אתה adonai attah, Thou art my prop, stay, or support. As the Messiah, or Son of God, Jesus derived his being and support from Jehovah; and the man Christ was supported by the eternal Divinity that dwelt within him, without which he could not have sustained the sufferings which he passed through, nor have made an atonement for the sin of the world; it is the suffering Messiah, or the Messiah in prospect of his sufferings, who here speaks. <div eID="gen18850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18851" type="x-p"/> My goodness extendeth not to thee - There are almost endless explanations of this clause; no man can read them without being confounded by them. The Septuagint read ὁτι των αγαθων μου ου χρειαν εχεις; Because thou dost not need my goods. The Vulgate follows the Septuagint. The Chaldee: My good is given only by thyself. <div eID="gen18851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18852" type="x-p"/> So the Syriac: My good is from thee. The Arabic: Thou dost not need my good works. And in this sense, with shades of difference, it has been understood by most commentators and critics. <div eID="gen18852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18853" type="x-p"/> Bishop Horsley translates, Thou art my good - not besides thee. Dr. Kennicott, My goodness is not without thee. <div eID="gen18853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18854" type="x-p"/> I think the words should be understood of what the Messiah was doing for men. My goodness, טובתי tobathi, "my bounty," is not to thee. What I am doing can add nothing to thy divinity; thou art not providing this astonishing sacrifice because thou canst derive any excellence from it: but this bounty extends to the saints - to all the spirits of just men made perfect, whose bodies are still in the earth; and to the excellent, אדירי addirey, "the noble or supereminent ones," those who through faith and patience inherit the promises. The saints and illustrious ones not only taste of my goodness, but enjoy my salvation. Perhaps angels themselves may be intended; they are not uninterested in the incarnation, passion, death, and resurrection of our Lord. They desire to look into these things; and the victories of the cross in the conversion of sinners cause joy among the angels of God. <div eID="gen18854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18855" type="x-p"/> The קדושים kedoshim, "saints," or consecrated persons, may refer to the first planters of Christianity, evangelists, apostles, etc., who were separated from all others, and consecrated to the great important work of preaching among the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of Christ. With these was all the desire, חפץ chephets, the good will and delight of Christ. In all their ministrations he was both with them and in them. <div eID="gen18855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18856" type="x-p"/> The passage, taken as referring to David, intimates that he abhorred the company of the profane and worthless, and delighted to associate with them that excelled in virtue. <div eID="gen18856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18857" type="x-p"/> On these two verses the translation and paraphrase of my old Psalter must not be forgotten: - <reference osisRef="Psa.16.1">Psa 16:1</reference> Conserva me, Domine, etc. <div eID="gen18857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18858" type="x-p"/> Trans. Kepe me Lord, for I hoped in the; I said til Lord, my God thou ert; for, of my gudes thu has na nede. <div eID="gen18858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18859" type="x-p"/> Par - The voice of Crist in his manhede; prayand til the fader, and sayand: Lord, fader, kepe me imang peplis, for I hoped in the, noght in me. I said til the, my God, thu ert in that, that I am man; for thu has no nede of my godes; bot I haf of the, al that I haf; here is the wil pride of men confounded; that evenes that thai haf ought of tham self bot syn. <reference osisRef="Psa.16.2">Psa 16:2</reference> Sanctis qui sunt in terra, etc. <div eID="gen18859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18860" type="x-p"/> Trans. Til halowes the qwilk er his land, he selcouthed all my willes in tham. <div eID="gen18860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18861" type="x-p"/> Par - Noght til wiked, bot til halows clene in saule, and depertid fra erdly bysynes, the qwilk er in his land: that es, that haf fested thair hope in the land of heven; and rotyd in luf: the qwilk hope es als anker in stremys of this werld. He selcouthed al my willes, that of wonderful, he made my willes, of dying and rysing, sett and fulfilled in tham: that es, in thair profete, qware in that feled qwat it profeted tham my mekenes that wild dye, and my myght to rise.
entries.12a2195653ff74639c0b61f6571c88a9b2e1f8f8: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen18861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18862" type="x-p"/> Their sorrows shall be multiplied that hasten after another god - The Chaldee has: "They multiply their idols, and afterwards hasten that they may offer their gifts." In the Hebrew text there is no word for God, and therefore Messiah or Savior might be as well substituted; and then the whole will refer to the unbelieving Jews. They would not have the true Christ; they have sought, and are seeking, another Messiah; and how amply fulfilled has the prophetic declaration been in them! Their sorrows have been multiplied for more than 1800 years. <div eID="gen18862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18863" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate and Septuagint, and after them the Ethiopic and Arabic, have given this clause a widely different turn: "their afflictions have been multiplied, and afterwards they have run swiftly;" referring to the suffering saints: the more they were afflicted and persecuted, the more fervent and prosperous they became. <div eID="gen18863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18864" type="x-p"/> Their drink-offerings of blood will I not offer - נסך nesech is a libation, whether of wine or water, poured out on the sacrifice. A drink-offering of blood is not a correct form of expression; it is rather the libation on the blood of the sacrifice already made. Coverdale translates the same; but Mathewes, who reformed his text in a few places, has Their brente offeringes of bloude, without much mending the text; though by this the exceptionable idea of a drink-offering of blood is avoided. As applicable to our Lord, here is an intimation that their libations and sacrifices should cease. None of these should exist under the Christian dispensation; Jesus Christ's offering upon the cross being the accomplishment and termination of all such sacrifices. <div eID="gen18864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18865" type="x-p"/> Nor take up their names into my lips - None of those sacrifices shall be mentioned with any kind of respect after the end of their institution shall have been accomplished; for sacrifice, offering, burnt-offering, and sacrifice for sin, such as are offered according to the law, God would no longer receive; therefore Jesus said; "Lo, I come to do thy will; a body hast thou prepared me." Since that time all these sacrifices have ceased. The old Psalter is curious: - <reference osisRef="Psa.16.4">Psa 16:4</reference> Multiplicate sunt infirmitates eorum; postea acceleraverunt. <div eID="gen18865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18866" type="x-p"/> Trans. Manyfaldend er thair sekenes: and sythen thai hasted thaim. <div eID="gen18866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18867" type="x-p"/> Par - That es at say; thai knew that thai war ful seke in body and saule, and sythen thai hasted tham til the Leche; for he that feles him seke, he sekes remedy. Il men wenes that thai er noght seke for thi that dye in thair syn. <div eID="gen18867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18868" type="x-p"/> Non congregabo conventicula eroum de sanguinibus, etc. <div eID="gen18868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18869" type="x-p"/> Trans. I sal noght gadyr the coventes of tha of blodes; ne I sal be menand of their names thurgh my lippis. <div eID="gen18869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18870" type="x-p"/> Par - That est at say, by the coventes of haly men, my servaundes sal nout fleschely, but gastly: for "blode" bytakyns syn and unclenes that that er in, that folous thair flesche, and the vanites of thair blode; that er comen of grete kyn. Ne I sal by menand of thair names; for thai er chaunged fra syn till ryghtwisnes on domesday, qwen I sal speke thrugh my lippes til thaim that haldes the name of wykednes: sa ye weryed til fyer with outen end.
entries.679678a4639e8ca449e7d332240698ec64f5c7d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen18870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18871" type="x-p"/> The Lord is the portion of mine inheritance - The Messiah speaks. Jehovah is the portion of mine inheritance; I seek no earthly good; I desire to do the will of God, and that only. It is God who has given me this lot - to redeem mankind - to have them for mine inheritance. From him I have received the cup of suffering, which I shall drink for their sake, through which I shall impart to them the cup of consolation. He, by the grace of God, has tasted death for every man; and he has instituted the cup of blessing to commemorate his passion and death.
entries.a61a26435d52e6befc6c8333eb9127bfa1cd0558: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen18871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18872" type="x-p"/> The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places - Here is an allusion to the ancient division of the land by lot among the Israelites, the breadth and length being ascertained by lines which were used in measuring. I have got a rich inheritance of immortal spirits; and I myself, as man, shall have a name above every name, and be raised to thy throne, on which I shall sit, and be admired in my saints to all eternity. <div eID="gen18872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18873" type="x-p"/> I have a goodly heritage - A Church, an innumerable multitude of saints, partakers of the Divine nature, and filled with all the fullness of God. And these shall dwell with me in the heaven of heavens to all eternity. The old Psalter: - <reference osisRef="Psa.16.5">Psa 16:5</reference> Dominus pars hereditatis mee et calicis mei, etc. <div eID="gen18873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18874" type="x-p"/> Trans. Lord es part of myn herytage and of my chalyce; thow ert that sal restore myn herytage til me. <div eID="gen18874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18875" type="x-p"/> Par - Lord the fader es part, that es, he es porcioun and mede of myn herytage; that es of haly men, qwam I weld in herytage. Other men cheses tham what tham lyst: my part es God, and he es part of my chalyce: that es, he es my copp of al my delyte and boor. Wereldys men drynkes the venemus lustes, and the drubly delytes of lychery and covatys: I in my halows sal drynk God; for thu ert fadyr that sal restore till me, that es, til my men, myn herytage, that thai lost in Adam: that es thu restores til tham the knawyng of my bryghthede. <reference osisRef="Psa.16.6">Psa 16:6</reference> Punes ceciderunt michi in preclaris, etc. <div eID="gen18875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18876" type="x-p"/> Trans. Strynges fel to me in ful bryght: for qwy, myn herytage is ful bryght til me. <div eID="gen18876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18877" type="x-p"/> Par - Strynges, that er merkes of my possessioun, in thi bryghtnes, fel als with cutte; als the possessioun of prestes and dekens in the alde law, was God; for qwy myn herytage, that es haly men es bryght til me of that seme layth and aute castyng til some of the werld, til me thai er fairer and bryght.
entries.6a24259b72715fe8b67cd744709203514a3d990f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen18877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18878" type="x-p"/> Who hath given me counsel - Jesus, as man, received all his knowledge and wisdom from God; <reference osisRef="Luk.2.40-Luk.2.52">Luk 2:40-52</reference>. And in him were hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. <div eID="gen18878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18879" type="x-p"/> My reins also instruct me - כליותי kilyothai, reins or kidneys, which from their retired situation in the body, says Parkhurst, and being hidden in fat, are often used in Scripture for the most secret workings and affections of the heart. <div eID="gen18879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18880" type="x-p"/> The kidneys and their fat were always to be burnt in sacrifice, to indicate that the most secret purposes and affections of the soul are to be devoted to God. <div eID="gen18880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18881" type="x-p"/> In the night seasons - That is, in the time of my passion, my secret purposes and determinations concerning the redemption of man support me. "For the joy that was set before him he endured the cross, despising the shame;" <reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">Heb 12:2</reference>.
entries.3a77ab8f73fc24e5d45fcc1c0d8465cd60561844: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen18881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18882" type="x-p"/> I have set the Lord always before me - This verse, and all to the end of <reference osisRef="Psa.16.11">Psa 16:11</reference>, are applied by St. Peter to the death and resurreetion of Christ. <reference osisRef="Act.2.25">Act 2:25</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen18882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18883" type="x-p"/> In all that our Lord did, said, or suffered, he kept the glory of the Father and the accomplishment of his purpose constantly in view. He tells us that he did not come down from heaven to do his own will, but the will of the Father who had sent him. See <reference osisRef="Joh.17.4">Joh 17:4</reference>. <div eID="gen18883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18884" type="x-p"/> He is at my right hand - That is, I have his constant presence, approbation, and support. All this is spoken by Christ as man. <div eID="gen18884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18885" type="x-p"/> I shall not be moved - Nothing can swerve me from my purpose; nothing can prevent me from fulfilling the Divine counsel, in reference to the salvation of men.
entries.f7c3294de9dd5607c82e31d40293e39e82484554: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen18885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18886" type="x-p"/> Therefore my heart is glad - Unutterably happy in God; always full of the Divine presence; because whatsoever I do pleaseth him. The man Christ Jesus must be constantly in communion with God, because he was without spot and blemish. <div eID="gen18886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18887" type="x-p"/> My glory rejoiceth - My tongue, so called by the Hebrews, (see <reference osisRef="Psa.57.8">Psa 57:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Psa.30.12">Psa 30:12</reference>), because it was bestowed on us to glorify God, and because it is our glory, being the instrument of expressing our thoughts by words. See Dodd. But soul bids as fair to be the meaning. See the notes on <reference osisRef="Act.2.25">Act 2:25</reference>, etc. <div eID="gen18887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18888" type="x-p"/> My flesh also shall rest in hope - There is no sense in which these and the following words can be spoken of David. Jesus, even on the cross, and breathing out his soul with his life, saw that his rest in the grave would be very short: just a sufficiency of time to prove the reality of his death, but not long enough to produce corruption; and this is well argued by St. Peter, <reference osisRef="Act.2.31">Act 2:31</reference>.
entries.56eacd37f0af984bc9c0833433bd109fc92a354b: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen18888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18889" type="x-p"/> Thine Holy One - This is in the plural number, חסידיך chasideycha, thy Holy Ones; but none of the versions translate it in the plural; and as it is in the singular number, חסידך chasidecha, in several ancient editions, among which is the Complutensian Polyglot, and no less than two hundred and sixty-four of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., and in the quotation by St. Peter, in <reference osisRef="Act.2.27">Act 2:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Act.13.35">Act 13:35</reference>, we may take it for granted that the present reading is a corruption; or that חסידיך is an emphatic singular. <div eID="gen18889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18890" type="x-p"/> As to leaving the soul In hell, it can only mean permitting the life of the Messiah to continue under the power of death; for שאול sheol signifies a pit, a ditch, the grave, or state of the dead. See the notes on the parallel places, <reference osisRef="Act.2.25">Act 2:25</reference> (note), etc. <div eID="gen18890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18891" type="x-p"/> See corruption - All human beings see corruption, because born in sin, and liable to the curse. The human body of Jesus Christ, as being without sin, saw no corruption.
entries.ec7f2909fffb7eff9d0941e1b2f8b7fef4708cff: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen18891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18892" type="x-p"/> Thou wilt show me the path of life - I first shall find the way out of the regions of death, to die no more. Thus Christ was the first fruits of them that slept. Several had before risen from the dead, but they died again. Jesus rose from the dead, and is alive for evermore. Jesus Christ's resurrection from the dead was the first entrance out of the grave to eternal life or lives, חיים chaiyim, for the word is in the plural, and with great propriety too, as this resurrection implies the life of the body, and the life of the rational soul also. <div eID="gen18892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18893" type="x-p"/> In thy presence - פניך paneycha, thy faces. Every holy soul has, throughout eternity, the beatific vision, i.e., "it sees God as he is," because it is like him; <reference osisRef="1Jn.3.2">1Jn 3:2</reference>. It drinks in beatification from the presence of the Eternal Trinity. <div eID="gen18893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18894" type="x-p"/> Thy right hand - The place of honor and dignity; repeatedly used in this sense in the Scriptures. <div eID="gen18894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18895" type="x-p"/> Pleasures for evermore - נצח netzach, onwardly; perpetually, continually, well expressed by our translation, ever and more; an eternal progression. Think of duration in the most extended and unlimited manner, and there is still more; more to be suffered in hell, and more to be enjoyed in heaven. Great God! grant that my readers may have this beatific sight; this eternal progression in unadulterated, unchangeable, and unlimited happiness! Hear this prayer for His sake, who found out the path of life, and who by his blood purchased an entrance into the holiest! Amen and Amen. <div eID="gen18895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18896" type="x-p"/> For the application of the whole Psalm to David, see the analysis at the end, which is a little altered from David's Harp Strung and Tuned. <div eID="gen18896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18897" type="x-p"/> The remains of this Psalm in the old Psalter are worthy to be inserted: - <reference osisRef="1Jn.3.7">1Jn 3:7</reference> Benedicam Dominum qui tribuit michi intellectum, etc. <div eID="gen18897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18898" type="x-p"/> Trans. I sal blis the Lord that gaf til me undirstandyng; and over that til the nyght, suyled me my neres. <div eID="gen18898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18899" type="x-p"/> Par - That es I sal luf the fader that hafs gyfen undyrstandyng til my servauntes, thurgh the qwilk the herytage of heven may be sene and welded; and aver that undyrstandyng, in the qwilk I saw, sais Crist, al sothefast thynges and haly. Of that I sal lof him that my nerys that es the Jewis of qwas kynd I toke flesch, that es my kyn snybbed me in wranges and temptaciounis, and passiouns, til the nyght, that es al the dede thai missaid hym, als so oure nerys; that es our fleschely delytes makes us worthy snybbyng til our dede; for perfytely may we noght be with outen syn, qwyles we lyf. <reference osisRef="1Jn.3.8">1Jn 3:8</reference> Providebam Dominum in conspectu meo, etc. <div eID="gen18899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18900" type="x-p"/> Trans. I pervaide God ay in my syght; for he es at the ryght hand til me, that I be nout styrred. <div eID="gen18900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18901" type="x-p"/> Par - And in al thys anguys I for gatt nout God: bot I pervayde hym ay in my syght; that es, I comande o mang passand thynges: I toke nout my nee fra hym that ay es; bot I fested it in hym, so that he was ay in my sight, and he es nout fyled in synnes that assyduely with the ee of his thoght, byhaldes God, for he es at the ryght hand of me: that I be noght styred; that es, he helps me in desyre of endless gudes, that I last stabil in hym, and for thi nane il thyng may haf mayster of me. <reference osisRef="1Jn.3.9">1Jn 3:9</reference> Propter hoc, elatum, est cor meum, et exultavit lingua mea, etc. <div eID="gen18901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18902" type="x-p"/> Trans. Thar fore gladded es my hert, and my toung joyed over that, and my flesch sal rest in hope. <div eID="gen18902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18903" type="x-p"/> Par - This es ful joy that in hert es resayved, and with toung schewed, and over that joy in hert and mouth, my flesch sal rest in hope of rysyng. <reference osisRef="1Jn.3.10">1Jn 3:10</reference> Quoniam non derelinques in Inferno animam meam, etc. <div eID="gen18903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18904" type="x-p"/> Trans. For thow sal noght lefe my Saule in hell, ne thu sal noght gyf thi Halow to se corrupcion. <div eID="gen18904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18905" type="x-p"/> Par - That es at say, the Saule that I haf als veray man, sal noght be left in hell; and my body that thu haloued, sal noght rote. Here men may knaw that this es goddes word; for other mens bodis rotes. <reference osisRef="1Jn.3.11">1Jn 3:11</reference> Notas michi fecisti vias vite, etc. <div eID="gen18905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18906" type="x-p"/> Trans. Knawen thu maked til me, the wayes of lyf: thou sal fil me of joy with thi face, delytynges in thi ryghth and in til the end. <div eID="gen18906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18907" type="x-p"/> Par - Knawen thu maked thurgh me till myne, the wayes of lyf, that es the wayes of mekenes and charite, that men came til heven thurgh mekenes, fra qwethyn thai fel thurgh Pryde: and thow sal ful fil me; that es, my servaundes, of joy with thi face; that es, in the syght of the, apertly; so that thai desyre nothing over, qwen thai af sene the, face til face, and ay til than delytynges til tham in way of this lyf. In thi ryght hand; that es thi favoure, and thi mercy the qwilk delytyngs ledys tham intil the ende, that es, in til perfectioun of endeles Blisfulhede. <div eID="gen18907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18908" type="x-p"/> I have given the whole of the translation and comment of this Psalm from this ancient Psalter, as a curious specimen of the doctrine and language of our northern neighbors in the thirteenth or fourteenth century.  <chapter eID="Ps.16"/> <div eID="gen18908" type="x-p"/>

entries.8d376ee2b6150207b893e959f704b36ef14e8dea: <div eID="gen9171" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Refuge in God, the Highest Good, in the Presence of Distress and of Death</title> <div sID="gen9172" type="x-p"/> The preceding Psalm closed with the words לא ימּוט; this word of promise is repeated in <reference osisRef="Ps.16.8">Psa 16:8</reference> as an utterance of faith in the mouth of David. We are here confronted by a pattern of the unchangeable believing confidence of a friend of God; for the writer of <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1-Ps.16.11">Psa 16:1-11</reference> is in danger of death, as is to be inferred from the prayer expressed in <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1">Psa 16:1</reference> and the expectation in Psa 16:10. But there is no trace of anything like bitter complaint, gloomy conflict, or hard struggle: the cry for help is immediately swallowed up by an overpowering and blessed consciousness and a bright hope. There reigns in the whole Psalm, a settled calm, an inward joy, and a joyous confidence, which is certain that everything that it can desire for the present and for the future it possesses in its God. <div eID="gen9172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9173" type="x-p"/> The Psalm is inscribed לדוד; and Hitzig also confesses that “David may be inferred from its language.” Whatever can mark a Psalm as Davidic we find combined in this Psalm: thoughts crowding together in compressed language, which becomes in <reference osisRef="Ps.16.4">Psa 16:4</reference> bold even to harshness, but then becomes clear and moves more rapidly; an antiquated, peculiar, and highly poetic impress (אדני, <hi type="italic">my Lord</hi>, מנת, נחלת, שׁפר, תּומיך); and a well-devised grouping of the strophes. In addition to all these, there are manifold points of contact with indisputably genuine Davidic Psalms (comp. e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Psa 16:5</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Psa 11:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Psa 16:10</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.4.4">Psa 4:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.16.11">Psa 16:11</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">Psa 17:15</reference>), and with indisputably ancient portions of the Pentateuch (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.13">Exo 23:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Exo 19:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.49.6">Gen 49:6</reference>). Scarcely any other Psalm shows so clearly as this, what deep roots psalm-poetry has struck into the Tôra, both as it regards the matter and the language. Concerning the circumstances of its composition, vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.30.1">Psa 30:1</reference>-12. <div eID="gen9173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9174" type="x-p"/> The superscription מכתּם לדוד, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1-Ps.16.11">Psa 16:1-11</reference> has in common with Psa 56:1. After the analogy of the other superscriptions, it must have a technical meaning. This at once militates against Hitzig’s explanation, that it is a poem hitherto unknown, an ἀνέκδοτον, according to the Arabic <hi type="italic">mâktum</hi>, hidden, secret, just as also against the meaning keimee'lion, which says nothing further to help us. The lxx translates it στηλογραφία (εἰς στηλογραφίαν), instead of which the Old Latin version has <hi type="italic">tituli inscriptio</hi> (Hesychius τίτλος· πτυχίον ἐπίγραμμα ἔχον). That this translation accords with the tradition is shown by that of the Targum גּליפא תריצא <hi type="italic">sculptura recta</hi> (not <hi type="italic">erecta</hi> as Hupfeld renders it). Both versions give the verb the meaning כּתם <hi type="italic">insculpere</hi>, which is supported both by a comparison with כּתב, cogn. חצב, עצב, and by חתם <hi type="italic">imprimere</hi> (<hi type="italic">sigillum</hi>). Moreover, the sin of Israel is called נכתּם in <reference osisRef="Jer.2.22">Jer 2:22</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.17.1">Psa 17:1</reference>) as being a deeply impressed spot, not to be wiped out. If we now look more closely into the <hi type="italic">Michtam</hi> Psalms as a whole, we find they have two prevailing features in common. Sometimes significant and remarkable words are introduced by אמרתּי, וימר, דּבּר, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.2">Psa 16:2</reference>; 58:12; <reference osisRef="Ps.60.8">Psa 60:8</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.38.10-Isa.38.11">Isa 38:10-11</reference> (in Hezekiah’s psalm, which is inscribed מכתּב = מכתּם as it is perhaps to be read); sometimes words of this character are repeated after the manner of a refrain, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.56.1-Ps.56.13">Psa 56:1-13</reference> : <hi type="italic">I will not fear, what can man do to me!</hi> in <reference osisRef="Ps.57.1-Ps.57.11">Psa 57:1-11</reference> : <hi type="italic">Be Thou exalted, Elohim, above the heavens, Thy glory above all the earth!</hi> and in Ps 59: <hi type="italic">For Elohim is my high tower, my merciful God</hi>. Hezekiah’s psalm unites this characteristic with the other. Accordingly מכתם, like ἐπίγραμμα,<note placement="foot">In modern Jewish poetry מכתם is actually the name for the epigram.</note> appears to mean first of all an inscription and then to be equivalent to an inscription-poem or epigram, a poem containing pithy sayings; since in the Psalms of this order some expressive sentence, after the style of an inscription or a motto on a monument, is brought prominently forward, by being either specially introduced or repeated as a refrain. <div eID="gen9174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9175" type="x-p"/> The strophe-schema is 5. 5. 6. 7. The last strophe, which has grown to seven lines, is an expression of joyous hopes in the face of death, which extend onward even into eternity.
entries.474d0aa3367a7d095601852fec4a51c4176928ff: <reference osisRef="Ps.16.1-Ps.16.3">Psa 16:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen9175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9176" type="x-p"/> The Psalm begins with a prayer that is based upon faith, the special meaning of which becomes clear from <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Psa 16:10</reference> : May God preserve him (which He is able to do as being אל, the Almighty, able to do all things), who has no other refuge in which he has hidden and will hide but Him. This short introit is excepted from the parallelism; so far therefore it is monostichic, - a sigh expressing everything in few words. And the emphatic pronunciation שׁמרני <hi type="italic">shāmereni</hi> harmonises with it; for it is to be read thus, just as in <reference osisRef="Ps.86.2">Psa 86:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.119.167">Psa 119:167</reference> <hi type="italic">shāmerah</hi> (cf. on <reference osisRef="Isa.38.14">Isa 38:14</reference> עשׁקה), according to the express testimony of the Masora.<note placement="foot">The Masora observes גרשין בספרא ב, i.e., twice in the Psalter שׁמרה is in the imperative, the <hi type="italic">o</hi> being displaced by <hi type="italic">Gaja (Metheg) </hi>and changed into <hi type="italic">aa</hi>, vid., Baer, <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi> p. 22f. In spite of this the grammarians are not agreed as to the pronunciation of the imperative and infinitive forms when so pointed. Luzzatto, like Lonzano, reads it <hi type="italic">shŏmereni</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen9176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9177" type="x-p"/> The text of the next two verses (so it appears) needs to be improved in two respects. The reading אמרתּ as addressed to the soul (Targ.), cf. Lam 3:24., is opposed by the absence of any mention of the thing addressed. It rests upon a misconception of the defective form of writing, אמרתּ (Ges. §44, rem. 4). Hitzig and Ewald (§190, <hi type="italic">d</hi>) suppose that in such cases a rejection of the final vowel, which really occurs in the language of the people, after the manner of the Aramaic (אמרת or אמרת), lies at the bottom of the form.
